c.tagline: A UNESCO colonial gem of pink-stone plazas, aqueduct arches, and wine country.

taxi.fareNote: Registered taxis and ride apps (Uber, DiDi) are widely used; confirm or agree the fare for unmetered street taxis before setting off.

emergency.note: 911 is Mexico's unified emergency number for police, fire, and ambulance.

solo.f: generally fine; one of Mexico's safest

hood_landmark.Centro Histórico: Plaza de Armas, Santiago de Querétaro

avoid.reason: Watch for petty theft in the Mercado de la Cruz area and on crowded buses; use normal night care outside the centro.

hood_desc: The UNESCO-listed colonial core of pedestrian andadores, pink-stone mansions, leafy plazas (Jardín Zenea, Plaza de Armas) and the best restaurants and nightlife; the obvious base for first-timers.
A historic hillside barrio around the Convent of the Holy Cross and the famous 74-arch aqueduct (Los Arcos), with viewpoints and a quieter, atmospheric feel just east of the center.
A central district anchored by the shady Alameda Hidalgo park, close to the historic center with hotels, transport, and an easy walkable base slightly off the busiest streets.
An upscale, leafy residential area north of the city known for its former hacienda, golf, security, and modern comfort; a calm, car-friendly base near shopping and business parks.
A modern planned suburb around a lake north of the center, home to universities, convention facilities, international hotels, and malls; quiet and green but a 20-30 min drive from downtown.

water.note: As across Mexico, drink bottled or purified water rather than tap.

transit.pay: Qrobús uses a rechargeable smart card bought and loaded at kiosks and stations; a ride costs about MXN 12 (~US$0.70). Some routes still accept cash - carry small change.
transit.hours: Buses generally run from around 5am to 10-11pm; late-night travel relies on taxis or ride apps.
transit.note: Querétaro has no metro or tram; the Qrobús bus network plus taxis and ride-hailing cover the city, while the compact historic center is best explored on foot.

transit.m: Qrobús airport shuttle (AIQ) to the Alameda, ~45-60 min
Authorized airport taxi to the center, 30-45 min

tip.r: ~10-15% at restaurants; rounding up for taxis and small services is common.

food.name: Enchiladas queretanas
food.desc: Tortillas dipped in a mild guajillo sauce, lightly fried, filled with queso fresco and onion, and served with potatoes, carrots and chicken.

places.name: Los Compadres
places.area: Centro Historico, near Plaza de Armas
places.note: Long-running antojitos counter locals send visitors to for the classic plate with potatoes and carrots.

places.name: Restaurante 1810
places.note: Terrace on the main square serving the traditional version for about three decades.

places.name: Huaraches y Gorditas Conchita
places.note: No-frills family spot repeatedly named for the most authentic enchiladas queretanas.

food.name: Gorditas de migajas
food.desc: Thick corn masa pockets kneaded with crisp pork crackling crumbs, griddled and stuffed with stews, salsa and nopales.

places.name: Gorditas del Andador
places.note: Pedestrian-street institution turning out migaja gorditas all day to a steady queue.

places.name: Gorditas El Guero y Lupita
places.note: Local favourite for the crunchy chicharron-crumb masa and generous guisado fillings.

places.name: Mercado de la Cruz
places.note: City market with several comal stands doing migajas and hand-pressed tortillas from dawn.

food.name: Nopales queretanos
food.desc: Cactus paddles from the surrounding semi-desert, grilled with onion and cheese or diced into salads and served alongside almost every local plate.

places.name: Mercado de la Cruz
places.note: Stalls sell them raw, cleaned and grilled, plus cooked-to-order nopal tacos.

places.name: Mercado Escobedo
places.note: Old neighbourhood market whose fondas plate nopales with cecina and pulque-based salsas.

places.name: Los Compadres
places.note: Serves nopales asados as a side with most antojitos, a good first taste.

food.name: Barbacoa de borrego
food.desc: Lamb wrapped in maguey leaves and pit-steamed overnight, eaten in tacos with consome on weekend mornings.

places.name: Mercado Escobedo
places.note: Weekend barbacoa stands with consome, best before mid-morning when it sells out.

places.name: Mercado de la Cruz
places.note: Saturday and Sunday pit-lamb counters, a Queretaro breakfast ritual.

places.name: Mercado Hidalgo
places.note: Central market with fondas doing barbacoa tacos and pancita alongside menudo.

food.name: Queso artesanal de Tequisquiapan
food.desc: Farmhouse cow and goat cheeses from the wine-and-cheese route around Tequisquiapan and Ezequiel Montes, often served with local quince paste.

places.name: Quesos VAI
places.area: Ezequiel Montes, Wine and Cheese Route
places.note: Family dairy on the Ruta del Queso y el Vino with tastings and a cheese-and-wine terrace.

places.name: Quesos Neole
places.note: Award-winning artisan creamery known for aged and washed-rind wheels.

places.name: Mercado de la Cruz
places.note: City-centre stalls carrying regional cheeses if you are not driving out to the valley.

food.name: Vino queretano
food.desc: Queretaro is Mexico second wine region; the high valleys around Tequisquiapan produce sparkling wine, malbec and blends poured all over the city.

places.name: Finca Sala Vive by Freixenet
places.note: Best-known sparkling-wine house in the valley, with cellar tours and tastings.

places.name: Vinedos La Redonda
places.note: Easy day-trip winery with a restaurant and by-the-glass flights.

places.name: Chucho El Roto
places.note: Popular central terrace with a strong list of Queretaro wines by the glass.

food.name: Cerveza artesanal Hercules
food.desc: Queretaro craft beer, brewed in a converted textile factory, spans pale ales to dark lagers and is poured across the historic centre.

places.name: Cerveceria Hercules
places.note: The brewery itself, with a big garden taproom inside the old mill complex.

places.name: Chucho El Roto
places.note: Central bar-restaurant with local taps and people-watching on the square.

places.name: Andador 5 de Mayo bars
places.note: Pedestrian strip lined with terraces pouring Queretaro craft taps at night.

landmarks: Acueducto de Querétaro (Los Arcos)
Seventy-four pink-stone arches march 1,280 metres across the city, an eighteenth-century aqueduct that remains Querétaro's proud emblem.
Plaza de Armas
An immaculate colonial square of clipped laurels, fountains and terrace restaurants, fronting the seat of viceregal government intrigue.
Templo y Ex-Convento de la Santa Cruz
On the hill where the city was founded, this convent hosted Emperor Maximilian's imprisonment and grows its legendary cross-thorned trees.
Templo de Santa Rosa de Viterbo
A flamboyant Mexican Baroque masterpiece of flying buttresses, pagoda-like tower and gilded interior, unlike any other church in Mexico.
Cerro de las Campanas
The hill where Emperor Maximilian faced the firing squad in 1867, marked by a memorial chapel and a colossal Juárez statue.
Teatro de la República
Mexico's 1917 Constitution was signed in this handsome 1852 theatre, which also heard the verdict condemning Maximilian.
Museo de Arte de Querétaro
A former Augustinian monastery whose fantastically carved Baroque cloister competes with the viceregal paintings displayed inside.
Jardín Zenea & Templo de San Francisco
The city's liveliest garden square, with its French kiosk and dancing retirees, backed by the orange-domed founding church.
Mirador de los Arcos
A hillside overlook framing the full sweep of the aqueduct's arches, most magical when floodlit against the evening sky.
Peña de Bernal
One of the world's tallest monoliths towers 350 metres over a wine-and-cheese pueblo mágico, an essential day trip from the city.

train.note: No passenger trains serve Querétaro today - the network is freight-only, though the planned Mexico City-Querétaro passenger line is under construction and would change that later this decade. For now travel is by coach or car.

bus.note: No international coaches. The Central de Autobuses has three terminals, with ETN (https://www.etn.com.mx/) and Primera Plus (https://www.primeraplus.com.mx/) running to Mexico City in about 3 hours, Guanajuato (2), San Miguel de Allende (1) and Guadalajara (5). It is one of the best-connected road hubs in the Bajío.

ferry.note: Querétaro is inland in the Bajío highlands with no navigable water, so there are no ferries.

half.name: San Miguel de Allende
half.blurb: A colonial hill town of cobblestone streets and a pink neo-Gothic parish church, known for its arts scene and expat community.

half.name: Tequisquiapan
half.blurb: A spa town built around thermal springs, with a colonial plaza, cheese and wine producers, and a Sunday crafts market.

half.name: Cadereyta de Montes
half.blurb: A small town near a regional botanical garden specializing in cacti, at the edge of the semi-desert Sierra Gorda foothills.

full.name: Jalpan de Serra
full.blurb: Gateway to the Sierra Gorda's five UNESCO-listed Franciscan missions, with an ornately carved 18th-century church facade at its center.
